messages.author: 253141a6efac547e
messages.subject: Knitr giving different p-values than in the console
parts:
So, I've been working in Rstudio (0.98.1062) on an example of distance based covariances.  Here's a gist of the code in .Rnw format for knitr:
https://gist.github.com/jebyrnes/b50e92e72f0ee1852cc5

In the console, I get a p-value of 0.005. When I knit it, I get something 0.755 So, it's not just a wee bit different, it's a problematically different.

I've consulted with the author of the energy package, and they have the same error.

Thoughts?

-Jarrett

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Knitr giving different p-values than in the console
parts:
Thanks for the investigation, JJ. I can reproduce 0.005 in RStudio
after setting the seed. I just read the documentation of dcov.test(),
and its says the P-value is obtained via permutation bootstrap. Then I
will not be surprised if the P-value is not exactly the same when you
run the test multiple times, however, a difference between 0.005 and
0.755 seems to be overwhelming. I started to doubt if the number of
replicates was too small, and then I discovered an interesting
phenomenon:

library(energy)
set.seed(123)
p = numeric(5)
for (i in 1:5) p[i] = with(activityDF, {
dcov.test(julian_day, temperature, R=10^i)$p.value
})

cbind(1:5, p)
p
[1,] 1 0.0909090909
[2,] 2 0.0099009901
[3,] 3 0.0009990010
[4,] 4 0.0000999900
[5,] 5 0.0000099999

The P-value decreases as we increase the number of replicates.
Moreover, if R is 10 times bigger, p becomes about 1/10 of the
previous p. I guess there might be a fundamental bug in the routine to
obtain P-value. You need to talk to the package author(s). BTW, also
note 0.0909090909 = 1/11, and basically p = 1/(R + 1). I think you
know what this implies in the context of permutation tests.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Web: http://yihui.name

messages.author: ce0c02d9f4a46b9b
messages.subject: Re: Knitr giving different p-values than in the console
parts:
I checked and the p-values computed by dcov.test are consistent and correct given the replicates that are returned by dcov.test. However, the numerical values of the replicates for this particular random number seed seem to be wrong. Strangely, by generating just one random number before the test, I can obtain the p-value 0.005 and the replicates look fine. Another fact is that the inconsistency is not there if I take the first 30 or first 60 rows of the data frame instead of all of it. 

The reason that the p-value here is decreasing with the number of replicates is that the observed value of the test statistic is very far from the null sampling distribution. The null sampling distribution should be invariant if we generate all permutations, so it should be approximately invariant if we generate 199. (The p-values decreasing with number of replicates is similar to what would happen if the null distribution is standard normal while the observed test statistic is say, 100.)  On the other hand, what happens with this data running in knitr is that unless the random number seed is set or updated in code appearing before the test, the replicates generated in the full example are simply wrong - not even close to the null distribution we get with a simple replicate() version of the test.

So I have one concrete example of apparently corrupted data in the replicates, which it seems must be internal to energy as some type of incompatibility with knitr, but so far I have been unable to come up with a single other example in which the sampling distribution of the replicates generated differs in knitr from the result when running the same code at the console.

Thanks to everyone that took time to look into this. It will be hard to find the cause of this issue but I am working on it.

    Maria

Many thanks to all for the help. I think that I have now solved the problem with 
my package and minutes ago submitted an update to CRAN. 

This is key:

On Sun, Oct 26, 2014 at 6:53 AM, JJ Allaire <j...@rstudio.com> wrote: 
> This has something to do with the state of the random number 
> generator. I noticed in energy.c that there are calls to 
> GetRNGState/PutRNGState around code that's upstream from computing the 
> p-value.

So, although energy.c is not used by dcov.test, I realized that this pair was
missing from dcov.c at the loop that generates replicates for dcov.test. This is 
an error that I may never have discovered without Jarrett's example. It is a good 
example to illustrate what can go wrong without that careful handling of random 
number generation.

In the new version of energy I have added GetRNGstate .. PutRNGstate outside
the sampling loop in dcov.c and now both the .Rnw and .Rmd versions of Jarrett's
example produce output consistent with that in the console. 

My guess is that knitr can update the random seed entering or leaving chunks
and maybe this is why my error is revealed in knitr and not otherwise. I realize that
my C code is not elegant and I'm working on a major update - but that will take much
more time to fully test.

I could not discover why the replicates appear to get corrupted in this scenario
because I could not find a way to debug the C code with knitr in control. When I
put the example into the "Examples" section of dcov.Rd to knit the dcov.Rmd 
file, it behaved like the console version. For now, I'll just have to settle for the 
correction.

I hope that this truly resolves the problem - Thanks again to everyone -

    Maria

messages.author: cc1ef8c8158d6b73
messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Knitr giving different p-values than in the console
parts:
Good point. However, in that case, the random seed was introduced by
the user in the first place, instead of knitr. What knitr did was
simply saving the random seed triggered by user's code. Maria's guess
was knitr touched the random seed somewhere internally, and I could
not think of any place in which knitr could possibly touch it by
itself. Some packages, however, do change the state of RNG, e.g.
ggplot2 uses runif() to decide whether to print a start-up message:

> ggplot2:::.onAttach
function (...)
{
if (!interactive() || stats::runif(1) > 0.1)
return()
tips <- c("Need help? Try the ggplot2 mailing list:
http://groups.google.com/group/ggplot2.",
paste("Find out what's changed in ggplot2 with\n", "news(Version == \"",
utils::packageVersion("ggplot2"), "\", package = \"ggplot2\")",
sep = ""), "Use suppressPackageStartupMessages to
eliminate package startup messages.")
tip <- sample(tips, 1)
packageStartupMessage(tip)
}
<environment: namespace:ggplot2>

But I do not recall any code in knitr related to RNG. Anyway, I do not
think the random state should dramatically change the result of a
permutation-base test, if the test is robust enough.

Regards,
Yihui
--
Yihui Xie <xiey...@gmail.com>
Web: http://yihui.name

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Knitr giving different p-values than in the console
parts:
I think that I see now - in fact there is a difference between knitr and the console
if knitr initially has no value set for .Random.seed. Generally .Random.seed
exists in the environment unless the user has deliberately removed it. As a result the
missing GetRNGstate() in my code has different consequences in knitr vs console:

Checking the source, in RNG.c the RNG_Init function should be called when
there is no .Random.seed, but without GetRNGstate() it might not be called:

static void Randomize(RNGtype kind)
{
/* Only called by  GetRNGstate() when there is no .Random.seed */
    RNG_Init(kind, TimeToSeed());
}

But, running in the console .Random.seed typically exists so the error of not calling 
RNG_Init does not happen.

I tried to reproduce the conditions in the following example. fx prints 0.00000 in
knitr, but at the console both fx and fy print the same result. 

```{r}
library(inline)

fxcode <- '
  double x = unif_rand();
  Rprintf("%f\\n", x);
  return R_NilValue;
'

fycode <- '
  GetRNGstate();
  double x = unif_rand();
  PutRNGstate();
  Rprintf("%f\\n", x);
  return R_NilValue;
' 

fx <- cxxfunction( signature(), fxcode)
fy <- cxxfunction( signature(), fycode)

invisible(fx())
invisible(fy())
```

messages.subject: Re: [knitr] Re: Knitr giving different p-values than in the console
parts:
I think the statement "Generally .Random.seed exists in the
environment" is not quite correct. It does not exist in my global
environment if I start a clean R session (hence fx() prints 0.00000 at
the R console). It may exist in your environment because you saved the
workspace image last time when you quit R. You need to verify it by an
absolutely clean R session, i.e.

R --vanilla

I do not know much about the low-level RNG stuff, but I know if you
want to initialize the random seed, you can call set.seed(NULL) in R,
which is basically what R does before RNG if the random seed does not
exist, and that is when .Random.seed starts to exist.

Regards,
Yihui
